ADM-201 tip: Flow is declarative automation. Apex is code. The exam always prefers Flow over Apex unless Flow literally can't do it.

When in doubt → choose Flow.

#SalesforceAdmin #ADM201

the Salesforce security model:

OWD = the floor
Roles = open it up
Profiles = the ceiling
Permission Sets = exceptions

get that order right and you've already answered 5+ exam questions

#SalesforceAdmin

salesforce has like 40+ different certs now.

honestly? 80% of job postings only care about three: Admin, PD1, and App Builder.

start there. don't get distracted by the niche ones until your employer pays for them.

if you're studying for the Admin exam, stop treating every topic equally.

Profiles/Permission Sets, Flow, OWD/Sharing, and Reports/Dashboards make up almost half your score.

know those cold. skim the rest.

cc: @salesforceben

the biggest mistake people make studying for ADM-201 is spending 2 weeks on 'Company Setup' (which is barely tested) and rushing through Flow (which is 20%+ of the exam).

look at the exam guide weights. study proportionally.

the salesforce admin exam costs $200.

the average salary bump for getting certified is $15k-$25k.

you are literally not going to find a better ROI in tech. just take the test.

taking the PD1 exam? if you see a question about slow Apex or performance issues, the answer is almost always 'bulkify your code'.

query outside loops. DML outside loops. use Maps. that's it.

entry admin: $65-80k | entry dev: $80-100k
senior admin: $100-130k | senior dev: $120-160k

devs start higher, but the gap shrinks a lot once you hit senior/architect levels.

studying for App Builder?

28% of the exam is just Process Automation (basically Flow). 

if you don't know the difference between a Screen Flow, Record-Triggered Flow, and Autolaunched Flow, don't take the test yet.

the best way to learn salesforce isn't reading trailhead modules. it's spinning up a free dev org and trying to build an app for a fake business.

break things. fix them. that's how you actually learn.

salesforce governor limits — the ones that actually show up on pd1:

100 soql queries per transaction
150 dml statements max
6mb heap size
10 second cpu limit

hit any of these = runtime exception. most pd1 failures trace back to not knowing this.

pattern i see a lot: admin cert → more scope → app builder → pd1 if they like code. not a rule just a shape.

Agentforce tip: if your agent keeps routing queries to the wrong Topic, the fix is almost never in the Action — it's in the Topic's Instructions. make them more specific about what the Topic handles and what it doesn't.

the Salesforce certification maintenance exam is not a full re-exam. it's 30-40 questions on what changed in the last release.

people treat it like a chore. it's actually the easiest 30 minutes you'll spend to keep a $200 cert active.

App Builder exam: if a question asks whether to use a Flow or a Validation Rule — Flow wins when you need to DO something (create a record, send an email). Validation Rule wins when you need to BLOCK something.

different jobs. don't confuse them.

something I wish I'd known earlier: you can take Salesforce certification exams from home. no test center required.

Kryterion Webassessor + a webcam + a quiet room. that's it.

no reason to delay.

Service Cloud Consultant tip: the difference between Entitlements and Milestones trips people up.

Entitlement = the service level agreement itself (e.g. 'you get 24hr support')
Milestone = the specific steps inside it (e.g. 'respond within 2 hours')

entitlements contain milestones.

if you're studying for Sales Cloud Consultant: Opportunity Teams vs Account Teams is a classic exam trap.

Opportunity Team = people collaborating on ONE deal
Account Team = people managing an ongoing customer relationship

they're not interchangeable on the exam.

the AI Associate exam is the shortest path to a Salesforce cert — 40 questions, 70% to pass, no prerequisites.

if you're job hunting and need something to add to your resume fast, this one takes about 2-3 weeks to prepare for.

PD1 tip: the exam will show you code and ask if it follows best practices.

red flag patterns to spot:
- SOQL in a loop
- DML in a loop
- no null check before accessing a list
- hardcoded record IDs or org-specific values

if you see any of those, the answer is 'no, this is wrong.'

a lot of people use Trailhead Superbadges to prepare for exams.

they're useful for hands-on practice but they test different things than the certification exam.

don't mistake completing a superbadge for being exam-ready. the exam tests specific scenario knowledge, not just whether you can follow instructions.

Integration Architect exam is brutal if you try to memorize every API.

better approach: understand the USE CASES for each integration pattern.

real-time response needed? REST.
bulk data? Bulk API.
event-driven? Platform Events.
complex B2B? EDI/MuleSoft.

know the 'when to use what,' not just the names.

Tableau Data Analyst tip: the exam tests whether you understand what chart type serves what purpose.

trend over time → line chart
part to whole → pie or donut
comparison across categories → bar chart
correlation between two measures → scatter plot

exam questions are usually scenario-based. know the use case, not just the chart name.

the Salesforce exam passing score is 65% for most certs. some are 63%, a few are 68%.

you don't need to get everything right. you need to get the high-weight sections right.

check the official exam guide for section weights before you study. study proportionally.

MuleSoft Integration Foundations is one of the more beginner-friendly certs if you're coming from a non-technical background.

40 questions. 70% passing score. covers integration concepts at a conceptual level.

it won't make you a MuleSoft developer, but it's a real cert and it's achievable in a few weeks.

experience Cloud Consultant tip: sharing rules and partner users trip everyone up.

partner users use the portal license. they follow the sharing model like internal users — OWD, role hierarchy, sharing rules all apply.

the exam loves to ask edge cases about what a partner user can and can't see.

Business Analyst cert tip: the exam cares less about Salesforce configuration and more about how you gather requirements and document processes.

if you've been studying the platform features, step back.

stakeholder interviews, user stories, process maps — that's what this exam is actually testing.

one thing that actually helps exam prep that nobody talks about: reading the wrong answer explanations more carefully than the right answer explanations.

you learn more from understanding WHY something is wrong than from confirming what's right.

makes sense in retrospect.

Platform Developer II (PD2) is the hardest Salesforce exam I've taken.

not because the concepts are more complex. because you have to write actual code during the exam in a dev org.

no multiple choice. you build things and submit them. completely different skill being tested.

the Strategy Designer cert is underrated for anyone working in Salesforce consulting.

it covers design thinking, user research, and translating business problems into solutions.

most Salesforce professionals have zero formal training in this. the cert fills a real gap.

Data Cloud tip: the exam heavily tests the difference between a Data Stream, a Data Lake Object, and a Data Model Object.

Data Stream = raw data coming in
Data Lake Object = raw data stored as-is
Data Model Object = structured, mapped version for activation

know that chain.

the CTA (Certified Technical Architect) is the only Salesforce cert that includes a live board review.

you present a solution to a panel of CTAs who ask hard questions.

it's not a written exam. it's closer to a PhD viva.

not for the faint-hearted, but the credential is real.

quick Study tip: when you're 2 weeks out from your exam, stop learning new things.

start reviewing what you already know.

your job at that point is to lock in what you've covered, not discover new gaps you don't have time to fill.

Sharing Visibility Architect tip: the exam loves questions about 'what's the most restrictive setting that still allows X?'

the answer usually involves understanding the cumulative effect of OWD + Role Hierarchy + Sharing Rules.

think in layers, not individual settings.

if you're going for the Application Architect credential, you need 4 certs: Data Architect, Sharing Visibility Architect, Dev Lifecycle Architect, and Integration Architect.

plan your sequence. Sharing Visibility and Data Architect first — they have the most foundational overlap.

CPQ Administrator tip: the Price Waterfall is probably the most tested concept.

List Price → Contracted Price → Discount → Net Price → Partner Price → Customer Price.

know that order. know what affects each step. at least 10 questions will touch this.

OmniStudio tip: the difference between OmniScript, FlexCard, and DataRaptor is fundamental.

OmniScript = guided multi-step process
FlexCard = contextual display of data
DataRaptor = data retrieval/transform layer

none of them do the other's job. exam questions exploit confusion between all three.

if you're studying for Field Service Consultant: Work Types, Work Orders, and Service Appointments are three different things and the exam will make you distinguish them.

Work Type = template for what work is done
Work Order = the specific job
Service Appointment = the scheduled time slot for that job

the Admin exam has a section called 'Change Management and Adoption' that most people skim.

don't.

it covers sandbox types, change sets, and how to manage releases. 5-8% of your score and most people treat it as an afterthought.

Marketing Cloud Consultant tip: the difference between Journey Builder and Automation Studio is a classic exam question.

Journey Builder = real-time, contact-based, event-triggered
Automation Studio = batch-based, scheduled, data-focused

wrong answer on this costs you easy points.

quick reality check: the Salesforce exam doesn't reward people who've done the most training.

it rewards people who understand the underlying concepts well enough to apply them to a scenario they've never seen before.

that's a different skill. train for that.

Revenue Cloud Consultant tip: the exam distinguishes heavily between Product Catalog, Price Book, and CPQ's Quote Line.

if you're coming from standard Sales Cloud, these concepts will feel familiar but they work differently in Revenue Cloud.

don't assume they're the same.

the Platform App Builder exam has 23% on 'Salesforce Mobile' — which catches most people off guard.

know the difference between Salesforce mobile app customization and Lightning pages optimized for mobile.

not the same thing. exam will ask you to choose between them.

if you're going for Pardot Specialist: the biggest trap is confusing Engagement Programs with Dynamic Lists.

Engagement Program = sends emails based on triggers/time delays
Dynamic List = automatically adds/removes prospects based on criteria

they often work together but they're not interchangeable.

Advanced Administrator tip: the exam assumes you already have Admin knowledge cold.

it goes straight to the harder stuff: complex sharing scenarios, advanced automation, sandbox management, and custom metadata vs custom settings.

if you're not fully confident with Admin basics, pass that first.

one thing that helps more than any study guide: find someone who took the exam recently and ask them what surprised them.

not for the specific questions (that's against the rules). for the type of questions and the areas they felt underprepared for.

real-world intel is underrated.

JavaScript Developer I tip: the exam is not just about JavaScript syntax.

big sections on: debugging tools, web components (LWC concepts), testing frameworks, and security best practices.

if you've only been studying JS syntax, you've been studying maybe 40% of the exam.

Identity & Access Management Architect: the hardest section is usually Identity Providers and Federation.

know the difference between SP-initiated and IdP-initiated SSO. know what SAML, OAuth, and OpenID Connect each do.

exam loves to give you a scenario and ask 'which protocol fits here?'

the Salesforce exam costs $200 per attempt in the US.

if you fail, retakes are also $200.

the cheapest way to study is to invest time upfront to understand the concepts properly, not to rush and retake.

the exam is testing comprehension. you can't shortcut that.

Education Cloud Consultant tip: Program Enrollment is a central object in EDA (Education Data Architecture).

know how it connects Contact → Account → Program → Term.

questions about how EDA models students, courses, and institutions will be scenario-based.

CRM Analytics (Einstein Analytics) tip: dataflows, recipes, and datasets are three different layers.

Dataflow = older way of preparing data
Recipe = newer, more flexible data prep in Data Manager
Dataset = the output that powers your lenses and dashboards

exam will test whether you know which layer to use for a given task.

Nonprofit Cloud Consultant tip: NPC (Nonprofit Cloud) and NPSP (Nonprofit Success Pack) are different products now.

if your study material doesn't clearly distinguish them, it might be outdated.

NPC is the newer managed package. NPSP is the legacy one. exam will reflect which one you're certified in.

slack Developer tip: the exam covers Bolt framework, Socket Mode, and event-based architecture.

most people go into this expecting it to be easy because 'it's just Slack.'

it's not easy. it tests actual event-driven development patterns. treat it like a real developer exam.

if you're choosing between taking a cert and getting hands-on project experience:

take the cert AND find a project.

neither alone is as powerful as both together.

certs get you the interview. project experience gets you the offer.

the MuleSoft Developer I exam is a lot of ground: API design, Mule runtime, DataWeave, connectors, error handling.

DataWeave gets underestimated. it's a full transformation language and at least 15-20% of exam questions touch it directly.

don't skim DataWeave.

the System Architect credential requires: Data Architect + Sharing Visibility Architect + Dev Lifecycle Architect + Integration Architect.

Application Architect requires different certs: Data + Sharing + Dev Lifecycle + Integration is technically the same 4.

wait — they're actually the same 4 certs. the Application Architect = System Architect = same credential. just different names historically.

exam tip that sounds obvious but isn't: read the ENTIRE question before looking at the answers.

Salesforce questions often have critical qualifiers at the end: 'without writing code,' 'with the least admin effort,' 'maintaining data integrity.'

that last clause changes which answer is correct.

UX Designer cert tip: the exam uses design thinking terminology specifically.

empathize → define → ideate → prototype → test.

know this framework cold and know which activities belong to each phase.

also know the difference between usability testing and A/B testing. exam distinguishes them.

Technical Architect (CTA) tip from someone who's studied the process:

the review board isn't testing whether your solution is perfect.

it's testing whether you can defend your decisions, acknowledge tradeoffs, and adjust your approach when challenged.

very different thing than passing a multiple choice exam.

the Salesforce certification list has 40+ certs now.

most of them nobody's ever heard of. a handful of them are on every job posting.

Admin, PD1, App Builder, Sales Cloud, Service Cloud, Agentforce Specialist.

learn the difference between 'this cert exists' and 'this cert gets you hired.'

if you're early in your Salesforce career and wondering which community to join:

Trailblazer Community (Salesforce's own forum) for technical questions.
Salesforce Ben's community for career stuff.
Salesforce LinkedIn groups for job openings.

all three serve different purposes.

final tip for anyone studying right now:

the exam is not designed to trick you. it's designed to test whether you understand the platform well enough to make good decisions on it.

if an answer feels sneaky or cheap, you're probably overthinking it. the right answer is usually the most Salesforce-standard one.
